done_state: A credential pattern present in an audit-plane line is redacted before that line's row is persisted, verified by reading the row back from the database file itself; any failure in one line's scrub-verify-publish chain results in zero rows for that line and a run that exits non-zero rather than reporting success; and the independent read-time credential check remains live and is promoted from advisory to contract.
requirement: PRD.md R8 (DEVH-13). Architecture: ARCHITECTURE.md 'R8 — write-time credential scrub, fail-closed'.

briefs.covers: SECURITY-PRIVACY-REVIEW.md F1, atlas/mcp/server.py MCP_VIEWS allowlist inversion (C7 amendment)
SECURITY-PRIVACY-REVIEW.md F2, QueryFacade.fetch() LIMIT pushdown (C8 amendment). Brief marker updated to this ticket; DEVH-27 and DEVH-49 remain cited here.

design_decision_reconciling_prd_and_arch: PRD.md R8 says a forced scrub failure means 'the ingest run shall exit non-zero and shall write no row'. The architecture, following muse, sets the unit of fail-closed atomicity at one audit line rather than one ingest run, so lines N-1 and N+1 still land when line N fails. These conflict and this freeze resolves them rather than inheriting both. Per-record atomicity is adopted, because it does not weaken the guarantee at all: the claim being protected is that no credential is persisted, and line N is never persisted either way, while lines N plus or minus one were independently verified clean on their own chains. Run-level abort would additionally have to decide what happens to rows already written, and either answer is worse -- rolling them back discards verified-clean audit data, and leaving them is the partial success the operator's fail-closed rule forbids by name. What does NOT survive from PRD.md R8 is the literal 'shall write no row', since other clean lines in the same run do get written; that clause is narrowed to the failing line. In exchange, and this is the half muse's note only gestured at, the run must not be allowed to report success: a dropped line is counted and the run exits non-zero at the end. Otherwise per-record atomicity converts a credential-leak failure into a silent record-loss failure, which is the same 'you only find out by looking' shape the rule exists to make impossible.

criteria.statement: A payload matching any credential pattern is redacted before persistence, and the redaction is confirmed by reading the stored row back from the database file rather than from any in-memory value.
criteria.verification: Build one synthetic audit line carrying a distinct planted match for EVERY pattern in atlas.warehouse.dq_runner.CREDENTIAL_PATTERNS, imported at test time rather than copied into the test, so that adding an eleventh pattern cannot leave this criterion silently testing ten. Ingest the line. Then open a NEW raw sqlite3 connection to the warehouse file on disk -- not the ingest connection, and not QueryFacade, whose own read path must not be able to satisfy a write-time criterion -- SELECT payload_json for that row, and assert no pattern matches. An implementation that scrubs only the first match found fails, because every pattern is planted in the same line.

criteria.statement: A scrub whose return value is clean while the bytes it persists are the original is caught and hard-fails, writing zero rows for that line.
criteria.verification: Deliberately inject a scrub that returns a cleaned string while writing the original payload. Ingest a line containing all planted patterns. Assert the ingest reports failure for that line and that a fresh connection to the database file finds zero rows for it. This is the criterion the architecture's toy model at r8_writetime_scrub_toy.py already proves is load-bearing: re-run in this session, its trap control hard-failed with all ten patterns detected, and a verification that trusted the scrub's return value would have passed the same bug clean.

criteria.statement: A scrub that raises hard-fails its line, leaving zero rows and no partial state.
criteria.verification: Force the scrub to raise. Assert the line's ingest reports failure and that a fresh connection to the database file finds zero rows for it. For temporary artifacts, do NOT scope the check to the warehouse directory: the reference implementation's write-temp step uses tempfile.mkstemp(), which without an explicit dir= argument resolves to the system temp directory, not the warehouse. A cleanup path that itself raises, or a process killed mid-cleanup, would leave a credential-bearing temp file in /tmp indefinitely and a warehouse-scoped check would never see it. Instead take an independent before/after snapshot of BOTH the warehouse directory AND the directory tempfile.gettempdir() actually resolves to at test time, and assert the two snapshots are identical after the forced failure. If the implementation passes an explicit dir= so temp files land beside the warehouse, the tempdir snapshot simply stays empty and the criterion still holds.

criteria.statement: The unit of atomicity is one line, and a dropped line cannot be silent: in a run where exactly one line fails, every other line still lands, the failing line writes nothing, the run reports a non-zero count of fail-closed drops, and the run exits non-zero.
criteria.verification: Two scenarios, both required, because one is not enough to distinguish a tally from a boolean. Scenario one: ingest five lines with exactly one rigged to fail. Assert, from a fresh connection to the database file, exactly four rows present, all four clean, the rigged line absent; assert the run's reported drop count equals 1 and its process exit status is non-zero. Scenario two: ingest six lines with exactly TWO rigged to fail. Assert exactly four rows present, both rigged lines absent, and the reported drop count equals 2, not 1 and not True. A drop_count implemented as `1 if any_line_failed else 0` passes scenario one and fails scenario two, which is the point of running both. An implementation that aborts the whole run fails the surviving-rows half of either scenario; one that drops lines and exits zero fails the non-silence half, which would convert this design's credential guarantee into undetected record loss.

criteria.statement: The independent read-time credential check stays live and is promoted from advisory to contract.
criteria.verification: check_audit_payload_credential_scan remains registered and executable after the write-time gate lands -- it is not retired as redundant, because a second differently-shaped check that does not share the write path's blind spots is the point. Its registration tuple in atlas/warehouse/tests/test_schema.py, currently ('audit_event', 'source', 'advisory', 'invariant'), reads 'contract' in the third position, and test_schema is green.

criteria.statement: A redacted row records that redaction occurred, stays wellformed, and an unredacted row is not marked as redacted.
criteria.verification: Per PRD.md N3, the fact of redaction must be recorded on the row rather than being inferable only from the absence of a secret. Ingest one line containing a planted credential and one clean line. Assert the redacted row carries a positive redaction marker and the clean row does not, so an implementation that sets the marker unconditionally fails. The wellformedness half must actually exercise the fields redaction touches, not merely run check_audit_envelope_wellformed and observe it pass: assert that the redacted row's payload_json still parses as JSON after substitution, that its payload_bytes still reflects the stored value rather than the pre-redaction length, and that the envelope check passes for both rows. If the marker needs a schema column, it is added to the DDL block in docs/atlas-architecture.md section 16, which atlas/warehouse/ddl.py extracts at import time, not to a second copy of the DDL in code.

criteria.statement: atlas/mcp/server.py's MCP_VIEWS is an explicit allowlist of what MCP may serve, not ALLOWED_VIEWS minus one excluded name -- SECURITY-PRIVACY-REVIEW.md F1. A view added to ALLOWED_VIEWS in future is invisible over MCP until someone deliberately admits it into MCP_VIEWS's own list.
criteria.verification: MCP_VIEWS's definition no longer derives from ALLOWED_VIEWS by set subtraction (grep confirms no 'ALLOWED_VIEWS if' construct remains). A test adds a synthetic view name to ALLOWED_VIEWS at test time and asserts it is NOT present in MCP_VIEWS unless separately added to the allowlist. Regression: every view servable over MCP before this change (ALLOWED_VIEWS minus v_fail_open_incident) is still servable after -- the allowlist's initial contents must be seeded from today's real set, not from an empty or arbitrary one.

criteria.statement: QueryFacade.fetch() bounds the SQL query itself with a server-side integer LIMIT parameter, never a Python-side slice applied after fetchall() has already materialized the whole view -- SECURITY-PRIVACY-REVIEW.md F2, the one finding exploitable by a caller today. The existing where_sql refusal (fetch() accepts no caller-supplied SQL fragment) is unaffected; LIMIT is bound as a parameter, never string-interpolated.
criteria.verification: Real warehouse fixture with more rows in a view than the requested limit. fetch(view_name, limit=N) returns exactly at most N rows AND its return shape is unchanged (columns, rows) whether or not limit is passed, so every existing zero-argument caller (monitoring's five fetch() call sites) stays correct with no change. Prove the bound is pushed into SQL, not applied after the fact: instrument or monkeypatch the cursor/connection so the test can observe how many rows the underlying sqlite3 cursor actually produces before any Python-side handling, and assert that count is exactly <= N -- a passing test built only on the RETURNED list's length would not catch a rows[:limit] slice after a full, unbounded fetchall(), which is the exact pre-fix defect. atlas_query_view (the one caller that needs to know whether more rows existed beyond the page) is responsible for its own truncation detection by requesting limit+1 from fetch() and trimming the last row itself -- fetch() itself does not fetch an extra row silently. where_sql is still refused when supplied (regression, unchanged from C1-C6's existing behavior). limit remains an int-only parameter; a non-integer, boolean, or out-of-range value raises QueryRefused rather than being silently coerced.

failure_criteria.statement: Verification trusts the value the scrub function returned instead of the bytes on disk. The scrub looks correct, every test is green, and a bug in the function's own persistence path ships a verbatim credential into the warehouse. This is not hypothetical: the architecture's toy model reproduced exactly this bug and only the disk read-back caught it.
failure_criteria.detection: C1 opens a new raw sqlite3 connection to the database file. C2 injects the bug deliberately and requires it to hard-fail.

failure_criteria.statement: Redaction is implemented in the serve path -- QueryFacade, a view definition -- rather than at write time. Every test that reads through the facade shows clean output, the stored payload is still verbatim, and any consumer reaching the table directly still sees the secret.
failure_criteria.detection: C1 forbids reading through QueryFacade and requires a raw connection to the file.

failure_criteria.statement: The scrub stops at the first pattern it matches. A line carrying one planted secret passes, and a real payload carrying several leaks all but one.
failure_criteria.detection: C1 plants a distinct match for every pattern in one line and asserts none survive.

failure_criteria.statement: The pattern list is copied into the test rather than imported. An eleventh pattern is added to CREDENTIAL_PATTERNS later, the test keeps asserting ten, and the new pattern is never verified as scrubbed by anything.
failure_criteria.detection: C1 requires the list be imported from atlas.warehouse.dq_runner at test time.

failure_criteria.statement: Per-record atomicity is implemented and a failed line is only logged. Rows keep flowing, the run exits zero, and record loss accumulates undetected -- the same 'you only find out by going to look' failure the fail-closed rule exists to prevent, moved from credential leak to silent data loss.
failure_criteria.detection: C4 requires a reported drop count and a non-zero process exit alongside the surviving four rows.

failure_criteria.statement: The read-time check is retired once the write-time gate lands, on the reasoning that it is now redundant. The system loses its only control that does not share the write path's blind spots, so a write-path bug becomes undetectable by construction.
failure_criteria.detection: C5 requires the check to remain registered and executable, and to be promoted rather than removed.

failure_criteria.statement: The redaction marker is set unconditionally, or derived from whether the scrub ran rather than whether it changed anything. Every row looks redacted, so the marker carries no information and cannot distinguish a scrubbed payload from a clean one.
failure_criteria.detection: C6 ingests a clean line alongside a credential-bearing one and requires the marker to differ.

failure_criteria.statement: A schema change for the marker is made by editing DDL in code. atlas/warehouse/ddl.py extracts the real DDL from docs/atlas-architecture.md section 16 at import time, so a second hand-maintained copy drifts silently from the source of record -- the exact failure ddl.py's own docstring says it exists to prevent.
failure_criteria.detection: C6 names the document section as the only place a column may be added.

failure_criteria.statement: A credential-bearing temporary file is left behind outside the warehouse directory. tempfile.mkstemp() with no dir= argument writes to the system temp directory, so a cleanup path that raises, or a process killed mid-cleanup, strands verbatim secrets in /tmp. A check scoped to the warehouse directory reports clean forever. Same shape as R23's self-reported-paths gap: check the disclosed location, miss the real one.
failure_criteria.detection: C3 snapshots both the warehouse directory and tempfile.gettempdir() as resolved at test time, before and after the forced failure.

failure_criteria.statement: The drop count is a boolean wearing a number's clothes -- `1 if any_line_failed else 0`, or a flag coerced to int. A single-failure scenario passes, the operator sees a plausible '1', and every run that drops two or more lines silently under-reports. The counting mechanism meant to make record loss visible becomes the thing hiding it.
failure_criteria.detection: C4 runs a second scenario with two rigged failures among six lines and requires the reported count to equal 2.

failure_criteria.statement: MCP_VIEWS is inverted to an allowlist, but the allowlist is seeded wrong -- empty, or missing a view that was legitimately servable before -- so the fix silently breaks existing MCP callers instead of just closing the future-addition gap.
failure_criteria.detection: C7's regression clause requires every view servable before (ALLOWED_VIEWS minus v_fail_open_incident) to still be servable after.

failure_criteria.statement: LIMIT is pushed into the SQL string via f-string/format interpolation of the caller-supplied limit value rather than a bound parameter, reopening exactly the caller-controlled-SQL crack fetch()'s where_sql refusal exists to close -- a limit value crafted as '1; DROP TABLE x' or similar would not be caught by an integer-only clamp applied to the wrong stage.
failure_criteria.detection: C8 requires LIMIT to be bound as a parameter, never string-interpolated, and requires where_sql's existing refusal to still hold.

failure_criteria.statement: The fix truncates the RETURNED row list to N rows (rows[:limit]) after fetchall() still ran unbounded -- the visible symptom (row count) looks fixed while the actual DoS cost (materializing the whole view) is unchanged.
failure_criteria.detection: C8 requires instrumenting the underlying cursor to prove the database itself never produces more than N rows, not just that the Python list handed back is short.

out_of_scope: Redacting safety.jsonl itself. The warehouse is a derived store and the append-only source is a separate decision with different reversibility, per PRD.md's own constraint.
R9's cwd-based ledger routing. Same write-time shape, separate requirement, separate ticket (DEVH-14), and blocked on a current measured count that does not exist yet.

Serve-time credential redaction in QueryFacade or in v_fail_open_incident's definition. Reasonable defense in depth on top of R8's write-time scrub, explicitly not a substitute for it, and not scoped here. Distinct from C8's LIMIT pushdown, which is a DoS bound, not a redaction mechanism.
Ingest throughput or latency tuning. N2's budget governs PreToolUse hooks, not the ingest path, which is not on the tool-call critical path.
Retiring or rewriting check_audit_ledger_partition_by_cwd. C5 covers the credential check only.
Any OTHER change to atlas/mcp/server.py beyond C7's MCP_VIEWS inversion. R7 (DEVH-12) is the STRIDE review of this file as a whole and is otherwise not R8's or this amendment's subject.
constraints: The unit of fail-closed atomicity is one audit line. See design_decision_reconciling_prd_and_architecture above -- this deviates from PRD.md R8's literal 'shall write no row' wording, deliberately and with the compensating non-silence requirement in C4.

audit.py's make_row_mapper keeps its existing behaviour and signature: it still produces the row dict. The new scrub is a separate module, atlas/ingest/audit_scrub.py, sitting between the mapper and the insert.
insert_audit_event_row keeps its signature. The architecture has it called against a temp table by the new harness rather than directly against the live warehouse; it is not rewritten.
Write-temp, verify by reading from disk through a fresh connection, then publish atomically. Never mutate a persisted row in place.
No new cross-component interface. Both files live under atlas/**, which is one declared component, so this stays intra-component exactly as the existing empty interfaces block already reasons.
Any schema change goes in the DDL block of docs/atlas-architecture.md section 16, which ddl.py extracts at import time. Never a second copy in Python.

This file sits at atlas/GOALS.json because component_root('atlas') resolves to 'atlas/'. Verified by running the resolver. Criteria here originally covered R8 only. The DEVH-49/DEVH-50 amendment (C7, C8) narrowly extends coverage to two named SECURITY-PRIVACY-REVIEW.md findings that happen to touch atlas/mcp/server.py and atlas/query/facade.py -- not a general reopening of R7 or R9 work under this freeze, which is still excluded beyond those two named fixes.

A stranded temp file there holds the unredacted payload.

amendments.from: One scenario: five lines, exactly one rigged to fail, assert drop count equals 1.
amendments.to: Two scenarios; the second uses six lines with two rigged failures and requires the reported count to equal 2.
amendments.reason: dev-harness-32 blind falsification of the R8 criteria. A single-failure scenario cannot distinguish a real tally from a boolean. Since C4's whole purpose is making dropped records non-silent, a miscounting count defeats the criterion from inside.

amendments.from: Asserted both rows pass check_audit_envelope_wellformed, which does not touch payload_json or the redaction marker and so added less coverage than it appeared to.

amendments.reason: dev-harness-32 blind falsification of the R8 criteria. Raised as minor and explicitly non-blocking, since the load-bearing marker-differs assertion was already sound. amendments.from: Required the underlying cursor to produce at most N rows (strictly <= N) before Python-side truncation, with no statement about fetch()'s return shape when limit is used.
amendments.to: Requires exactly <= N rows AND requires fetch()'s return shape to stay (columns, rows) regardless of whether limit is passed -- truncation detection ('were there more rows than the page') is pushed to the one caller that needs it, atlas_query_view, which requests limit+1 from fetch() and trims the extra row itself. fetch() stays a minimal, honest LIMIT pushdown with no hidden extra-row fetching and no change to what any existing zero-argument caller sees.
amendments.reason: Self-caught twice while designing the fix, before any implementation or verification ran, per this project's own real-execution-only standard (same discipline as docs/GOALS.json's C1 and this same file's own prior C3 amendment). First pass wrongly put the +1/truncation logic inside fetch() itself and returned a 3-tuple only when limit was given, which would have broken every existing 2-value-unpack caller (monitoring's five fetch() call sites, atlas/mcp/server.py's own) the moment they passed limit, and behaved inconsistently based on an argument's presence. Reworked so fetch()'s contract never changes shape; only atlas_query_view, which already owns the 'truncated' field in its own response and is the only real limit-passing caller today, does the +1 request and trim.
amendments.requested_by: dev-harness-run2 (this session, self-caught during scoping, before implementation)
